result:
REST maps resources to URLs and HTTP verbs, so caching works at every layer (browser, CDN, proxy) for free. Status codes, tooling, and mental models are universal, and each endpoint has a predictable cost, which makes rate limiting and monitoring simple. The downsides: clients over-fetch (fat payloads) or under-fetch (N round trips to assemble one screen). Versioning and endpoint sprawl grow as client needs diverge.

GraphQL gives you one endpoint and a typed schema, and clients ask for exactly the fields they need. That means fewer round trips, no over-fetching, strong introspection and codegen, and the schema can evolve by deprecating fields instead of shipping versions. The costs fall on the server. HTTP caching mostly breaks because everything is a POST to one URL, so you need client caches or persisted queries. Arbitrary queries make performance unpredictable: N+1 resolver problems need DataLoader-style batching, and abuse needs depth and complexity limits. Errors come back as 200 with an `errors` array, field-level authorization is more work, and file uploads and streaming are awkward.

Verdict: default to REST for public APIs, simple CRUD, cache-heavy reads, or small teams. Pick GraphQL when you have several clients (web, mobile) with divergent data needs over a deeply relational domain, and you can afford the server-side complexity. Middle ground: REST with sparse fieldsets and an `include` parameter, or a GraphQL backend-for-frontend layered over REST services.
